pos: n. (a settlement smaller than a city, often unwalled; rendering Hebrew ir, Greek kome)
etymology: Old English tūn, an enclosure, a farmstead; the word grew from the fence to what the fence held. The Greek kome is a village as against a walled city.
biblical_def: Rahab's house “was upon the town wall” (Jos 2:15). “The elders of the town trembled” at Samuel's coming to Bethlehem (1Sa 16:4). Christ sent the twelve “into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter” (Mat 10:11), led the blind man of Bethsaida “out of the town” and told him afterward, “Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town” (Mar 8:23, 26). Bethlehem is “the town where David was” (John 7:42), and Bethany “the town of Mary and her sister Martha” (John 11:1). Habakkuk pronounces “Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!” (Hab 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines town as any collection of houses larger than a village; in the Scriptures, a walled or fenced place.
webster_full: TOWN, n. Originally, a walled or fortified place; a collection of houses inclosed with walls, hedges or palisades.
2. Any collection of houses, larger than a village.
3. In the United States, the whole territory within certain limits, a township.
corruption_summary: Christ's silence to the man of Bethsaida is read as false modesty, when Bethsaida was a town He had already pronounced woe upon.
corruption_paragraphs: The blind man of Mark 8 is led out of the town before he is healed and told not to go back into it after, and the reader assumes the Lord is being shy about miracles. He had already said of that town, “Woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago” (Mat 11:21). A town that has seen the works and not repented is not given more works to ignore. Judgment in the Gospels is often quiet: the Lord simply stops performing for the people who will not believe, and the healed man is sent home by another road.
roots_summary: Hebrew ir (H5892), a city, town; Greek kome (G2968), a village, unwalled town; komopolis (G2969), a town.
roots_lines: Hebrew ir (H5892) — city, town; 1 Samuel 16:4, Habakkuk 2:12, Joshua 2:15.
Greek kome (G2968) — village, town; Matthew 10:11, Mark 8:23, 8:26, John 7:42, 11:1, 11:30.
Greek komopolis (G2969) — a country town; Mark 1:38 only.
usage: “Into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter” — the twelve sent out.
“Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town” — Bethsaida cut off from further signs.
“Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood” — Habakkuk on the Chaldean.

pos: n. (a line of things set in order; rendering Hebrew tur and ma'areket)
etymology: Old English rāw, a line. The breastplate's stones, the shewbread, and Solomon's cedar beams were all set in rows.
biblical_def: The breastplate of judgment held “four rows of stones: the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle” (Exo 28:17), through the fourth row of “a beryl, and an onyx, and a jasper” (Exo 28:20) — twelve stones for twelve tribes, carried on the high priest's heart. The shewbread was set “in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the LORD” (Lev 24:6). Solomon's inner court had “three rows of hewed stone, and a row of cedar beams” (1Ki 6:36). The bride's cheeks “are comely with rows of jewels” (Sng 1:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines row as a series of persons or things arranged in a continued line; a rank; a file.
webster_full: ROW, n. A series of persons or things arranged in a continued line; a line; a rank; a file; as a row of trees; a row of houses.
corruption_summary: The rows of the breastplate are read for gemstone mysticism, and the text says whose names were on them and where they were carried.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 28 lists twelve stones in four rows, and the modern reader goes looking for what each stone means. The chapter tells him: “the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names” (v. 21), and Aaron “shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth in unto the holy place” (v. 29). The rows are the tribes, and the point of the rows is that they were on the heart of the man who went in before God. Christ our High Priest carries His people the same way, by name, in rows, and no stone in the breastplate had a power of its own.
roots_summary: Hebrew tur (H2905), a row, course; ma'areket (H4635), an arrangement, row; tor (H8447), a row, plait.
roots_lines: Hebrew tur (H2905) — a row, course of stones; Exodus 28:17–20, 39:10–13, 1 Kings 6:36, 7:2–4, Ezekiel 46:23.
Hebrew ma'areket (H4635) — a row, the shewbread's arrangement; Leviticus 24:6–7.
Hebrew tor (H8447) — a row, string of jewels; Song of Solomon 1:10–11.
usage: “Four rows of stones” — twelve names on one heart.
“Two rows, six on a row” — the shewbread before the LORD.
“Three rows of hewed stone, and a row of cedar beams” — Solomon's court.

pos: n. (ground grain, flour; rendering Hebrew qemach, Greek aleuron)
etymology: Old English melu, from the root of mill and grind. The other meal, a sitting at food, is a different Old English word; the Authorized Version's meal is always flour.
biblical_def: Sarah was told to “Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes” for the three visitors (Gen 18:6). The widow of Zarephath had “an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse” (1Ki 17:12), and heard the word, “The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain” (1Ki 17:14). Elisha cast meal into the pot of death (2Ki 4:41). The Lord likened the kingdom to leaven “which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened” (Mat 13:33). Hosea's standing corn “hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal” (Hos 8:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines meal as the substance of edible grain ground to fine particles, and not bolted or sifted.
webster_full: MEAL, n. The substance of edible grain ground to fine particles, and not bolted or sifted. The word is applied to the ground corn of wheat, rye, barley, oats, maize, &c.
2. A portion of food taken at one time; a repast.
corruption_summary: The barrel of meal is preached as a seed-faith formula, when the widow was fed by a word she did not choose to obey and could not have bargained for.
corruption_paragraphs: The widow's handful of meal has been made the text of a transaction: give your last to the man of God and the barrel will never fail. Read the chapter. She was a Gentile in Sidon, chosen before Elijah arrived (“I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee”), she expected to die that day, and the miracle was announced to her as a word from the LORD God of Israel before she baked anything. Her obedience was real and it was rewarded, but the ground of the supply was the word, not the size of the gift, and the Lord's own use of the story is not about giving at all: “many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias… but unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon” (Luk 4:25–26) — a text on sovereign election that got Him thrown out of Nazareth.
roots_summary: Hebrew qemach (H7058), meal, flour; soleth (H5560), fine flour; Greek aleuron (G224), meal.
roots_lines: Hebrew qemach (H7058) — meal, flour; Genesis 18:6, 1 Kings 17:12–16, 2 Kings 4:41, Numbers 5:15, Hosea 8:7, Isaiah 47:2.
Hebrew soleth (H5560) — fine flour; Genesis 18:6, “fine meal.”
Greek aleuron (G224) — meal, wheat flour; Matthew 13:33, Luke 13:21.
usage: “The barrel of meal shall not waste” — a word before the baking.
“Three measures of fine meal” — Sarah's cakes for the three visitors, and the measure in the parable.
“The bud shall yield no meal” — Hosea's harvest of wind.

pos: n. pl. (those who take by violence; rendering Hebrew parits, shodad, and gedud, Greek lestes)
etymology: Old French rober, from a Germanic root meaning to plunder. The Greek lestes is a bandit with a knife, not a pickpocket.
biblical_def: Christ said of all who came before Him claiming His office, “All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them” (John 10:8). Jeremiah asked of the temple, “Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jer 7:11) — the sentence the Lord quoted when He cleansed it. Job observes that “the tabernacles of robbers prosper” (Job 12:6). Hosea's priests are “as troops of robbers” waiting for a man (Hos 6:9). Paul was “in perils of robbers” (2Co 11:26), and the town clerk of Ephesus certified that Paul's companions were “neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers” (Act 19:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines robber as one that robs; one that takes goods or money from the person of another by force or menaces.
webster_full: ROBBER, n. One that robs; one that takes goods or money from the person of another by force or menaces, and with a felonious intent.
2. In a looser sense, one who takes that to which he has no right; one who steals; a plunderer.
corruption_summary: A den of robbers is read as a complaint about commerce in the temple, when Jeremiah used it of worshippers who sinned all week and hid in the house on the sabbath.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 7:11 is not about the money-changers; there were none in Jeremiah's temple. The verse before it is: “Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal… and come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, We are delivered to do all these abominations?” A den is where robbers go after the robbery, to be safe. The people were using the house of the LORD as a hideout — sinning in the city and taking sanctuary in the sanctuary — and when the Lord quoted the verse over the tables in Matthew 21 He was charging Jerusalem with the same thing, with the commerce as the visible symptom. The church that is a refuge for the impenitent, where a man can do what he likes all week because he attends on the Lord's day, is a den in the prophet's exact sense.
roots_summary: Hebrew parits (H6530), a violent one, robber; shodad (H7703), a destroyer, spoiler; gedud (H1416), a marauding band; Greek lestes (G3027), a bandit; hierosulos (G2417), a robber of temples.
roots_lines: Hebrew parits (H6530) — violent, a robber; Jeremiah 7:11, Ezekiel 7:22, Daniel 11:14.
Hebrew shodad (H7703) — to spoil, a spoiler; Job 12:6, Obadiah 1:5; gedud (H1416), a troop; Hosea 6:9, 7:1.
Greek lestes (G3027) — a robber, bandit; John 10:8, 2 Corinthians 11:26, Matthew 21:13; hierosulos (G2417), Acts 19:37.
usage: “A den of robbers” — a hideout for men who sinned all week.
“All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers” — every rival shepherd.
“In perils of robbers” — Paul's roads.

pos: n. pl. (labourers, craftsmen; rendering Hebrew oseh melakah and charash, Greek ergates)
etymology: Work + men. The Hebrew phrase is literally the doers of the work — the men into whose hands the temple money was put.
biblical_def: When Jehoash repaired the temple, the money was given “to the workmen, and repaired therewith the house of the LORD” (2Ki 12:14), and “they reckoned not with the men, into whose hand they delivered the money to be bestowed on workmen: for they dealt faithfully” (2Ki 12:15). Under Josiah the money went “into the hand of the workmen that had the oversight of the house of the LORD” (2Ch 34:10). David told Solomon, “there are workmen with thee in abundance, hewers and workers of stone and timber” (1Ch 22:15). Isaiah says of the idol-makers, “the workmen, they are of men” (Isa 44:11). Jael's hand went “to the workmen's hammer” (Jdg 5:26). Demetrius called together “the workmen of like occupation” against Paul (Act 19:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines workman as any man employed in labor, whether in tillage or manufactures; particularly, a man skilled in his craft.
webster_full: WORKMAN, n. Any man employed in labor, whether in tillage or manufactures.
2. By way of eminence, a skillful artificer or laborer.
corruption_summary: Accountability is treated as distrust, and the workmen of 2 Kings 12 were not audited because they had proved faithful.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Kings 12:15 is quoted both ways. Some read it as a rule against oversight — the priests did not reckon with the workmen, so the church should not reckon with its stewards. The verse gives the reason: “for they dealt faithfully.” The absence of an audit was a verdict on men already known, not a policy for men unknown, and the chapter opened with a chest, a hole bored in its lid, and the king's scribe and the high priest counting the money together (v. 9–10), which is the policy. Isaiah 44:11 sees the other kind of workman: the men who make a god and are themselves only men, whose work is the measure of the thing they worship. What a workman builds is worth exactly what his hands are worth, and an idol never rises above its maker.
roots_summary: Hebrew oseh melakah (H6213, H4399), doers of the work; charash (H2796), a craftsman, artificer; Greek ergates (G2040), a labourer.
roots_lines: Hebrew asah melakah (H6213 with H4399) — doers of the work; 2 Kings 12:14–15, 2 Chronicles 24:13, 34:10, 34:17.
Hebrew charash (H2796) — craftsman, engraver; Isaiah 44:11, 1 Chronicles 22:15, Hosea 8:6.
Greek ergates (G2040) — labourer, workman; Acts 19:25, Matthew 9:37, 2 Timothy 2:15.
usage: “They reckoned not with the men… for they dealt faithfully” — trust earned, not assumed.
“The workmen, they are of men” — an idol no better than its maker.
“The workmen of like occupation” — Demetrius's union against the gospel.

pos: n. pl. (male household servants; rendering Hebrew abadim, Greek paides)
etymology: Men + servants, the Authorized Version's plural for the male bondservants of a household, paired nearly always with maidservants.
biblical_def: Abram's wealth in Egypt was “sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants” (Gen 12:16), and Abimelech restored Sarah with “menservants, and womenservants” (Gen 20:14). Jacob sent word to Esau, “I have oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants” (Gen 32:5). The Law's rejoicing before the LORD included “your menservants, and your maidservants, and the Levite” (Deu 12:12). Samuel warned that a king “will take your menservants, and your maidservants” (1Sa 8:16). Gehazi's greed was named in the same list — “menservants, and maidservants” (2Ki 5:26). And the unfaithful steward in the parable begins “to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken” (Luk 12:45).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines manservant as a male servant.
webster_full: MANSERVANT, n. A male servant.
corruption_summary: The menservants are read as proof that Scripture blesses slavery, and the Law made them guests at the feast and the parable made beating them the mark of the steward who will be cut in sunder.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 12:12 puts the menservants at the table: “ye shall rejoice before the LORD your God, ye, and your sons, and your daughters, and your menservants, and your maidservants.” The bondman of Israel rested on the sabbath (Exo 20:10), ate the feast, went free in the seventh year with a gift (Deu 15:12–14), and could not be returned to a master he had fled (Deu 23:15). The modern charge that the Bible endorses the slave trade has to get past the verse that made kidnapping a man a capital crime (Exo 21:16). Luke 12:45 gives the Lord's view of the master who beats his menservants: he is the steward who said in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming, and his portion is with the unbelievers.
roots_summary: Hebrew ebed (H5650), a servant, bondman; Greek pais (G3816), a boy, servant.
roots_lines: Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant, bondman; Genesis 12:16, 20:14, 32:5, Deuteronomy 12:12, 1 Samuel 8:16, 2 Kings 5:26.
Greek pais (G3816) — servant, boy; Luke 12:45, “the menservants and maidens.”
usage: “Your menservants, and your maidservants” — guests at the LORD's feast.
“He will take your menservants” — Samuel's warning about kings.
“To beat the menservants and maidens” — the steward who thought his lord delayed.

pos: n. pl. (in the AV only in the phrase liers in wait, an ambush; rendering Hebrew arab)
etymology: From lie, to remain in place. The Authorized Version never uses the word alone; liers in wait is its rendering of the Hebrew participle for men set in ambush.
biblical_def: Joshua “set the people, even all the host that was on the north of the city, and their liers in wait on the west of the city” against Ai (Jos 8:13), and the men of Ai “wist not that there were liers in ambush against him behind the city” (Jos 8:14). The men of Shechem “set liers in wait for” Abimelech in the mountains (Jdg 9:25). Delilah had “liers in wait abiding in the chamber” while she bound Samson (Jdg 16:12). “Israel set liers in wait round about Gibeah” (Jdg 20:29), and they “came forth out of their places” when the Benjamites were drawn off (Jdg 20:33). Babylon is told, “prepare the liers in wait” (Jer 51:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lier as one who lies down; one who rests or remains; as, a lier in wait or in ambush.
webster_full: LIER, n. One who lies down; one who rests or remains; as a lier in wait or in ambush.
corruption_summary: Delilah's liers in wait are read as a story about a strong man's weakness for women, when the text shows a man who knew the ambush was in the room and stayed.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 16 repeats the phrase for a reason. Three times Delilah asks the secret, three times Samson lies, and each time “there were liers in wait abiding in the chamber” and each time she cries, “The Philistines be upon thee, Samson.” He knew. After the first cry he knew there were men behind the curtain; after the second he knew what she was; and he told her the truth the fourth time anyway. The modern reading pities him as a man undone by passion. The chapter shows a man who saw the ambush spring three times and lay down again in the same room, and Proverbs has a name for that: a bird hasting to the snare, and knowing not that it is for his life. Ambush is a fair tactic of war, and Joshua used it at Ai by God's command; it is a fatal tactic of temptation, because the liers in wait only need a man who will not leave the chamber.
roots_summary: Hebrew arab (H693), to lie in wait, ambush; oreb (H696), an ambush.
roots_lines: Hebrew arab (H693), participle — liers in wait; Joshua 8:13–14, Judges 9:25, 16:12, 20:29–37, Ezra 8:31.
Hebrew oreb (H696) — an ambush, lier in wait; Jeremiah 51:12.
usage: “Their liers in wait on the west of the city” — Ai taken by ambush at God's command.
“Liers in wait abiding in the chamber” — Samson knew, and stayed.
“Prepare the liers in wait” — Babylon's fall arranged.

pos: n. pl. (the tent pegs of the tabernacle; rendering Hebrew yathed)
etymology: Old English pinn, a peg. The Hebrew yathed is the tent peg — the same word for Jael's nail and for the nail fastened in a sure place.
biblical_def: The tabernacle stood by them: “All the vessels of the tabernacle in all the service thereof, and all the pins thereof, and all the pins of the court, shall be of brass” (Exo 27:19); “The pins of the tabernacle, and the pins of the court, and their cords” (Exo 35:18); “all the pins of the tabernacle, and of the court round about, were of brass” (Exo 38:20). The Merarites carried “the pillars of the court round about, and their sockets, and their pins, and their cords” (Num 3:37; 4:32). Isaiah lists the “crisping pins” among the finery of the daughters of Zion (Isa 3:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pin as a small pointed instrument for fastening; a peg; a bolt.
webster_full: PIN, n. A small pointed instrument of brass or other metal, used for fastening clothes.
2. A peg used in fastening; as the pins of a tent.
3. A thing of little value; a trifle.
corruption_summary: The pins are skipped as the dullest verses in Exodus, and the whole tent depended on them.
corruption_paragraphs: Nobody preaches on the pins. They are listed four times in Exodus and twice in Numbers, always at the end of the inventory, and the reader who has admired the ark and the candlestick lets his eye slide past the brass pegs. But the tabernacle was a tent, and a tent is held to the ground by its pins; the gold within depended on the brass without. A family of Levites was assigned to carry them (Num 3:37) and to know exactly where each one went, and God counted them worth naming. The same Hebrew word is Jael's nail through Sisera's temples (Jdg 4:21) and the nail fastened “in a sure place” on which the glory of a house is hung (Isa 22:23) — a small thing that bears a great weight. The church has always had more candlesticks than pins, and it has never once stood without the pins.
roots_summary: Hebrew yathed (H3489), a peg, pin, nail; charit (H2754), a bag, purse, rendered crisping pins.
roots_lines: Hebrew yathed (H3489) — tent peg, pin, nail; Exodus 27:19, 35:18, 38:20, Numbers 3:37, 4:32, Judges 4:21, Isaiah 22:23, Ezekiel 15:3.
Hebrew charit (H2754) — a purse, bag; Isaiah 3:22, “crisping pins.”
usage: “All the pins thereof, and all the pins of the court, shall be of brass” — the tent held to the ground.
“Their sockets, and their pins, and their cords” — the Merarites' load.
“The crisping pins” — the finery Isaiah counted before it was taken away.

pos: v. (to carry on the body as clothing; to waste away by use; rendering Hebrew labash and nasa, Aramaic bela, Greek phoreo)
etymology: Old English werian, to clothe oneself. The second sense, to wear away, grew from the first: what is worn is worn down.
biblical_def: The Law forbids that a woman “wear that which pertaineth unto a man” (Deu 22:5) and that anyone “wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together” (Deu 22:11). Jethro warned Moses, “Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee: for this thing is too heavy for thee” (Exo 18:18). Job says “the waters wear the stones” (Job 14:19). Daniel's little horn “shall wear out the saints of the most High” (Dan 7:25). The Lord asked of John, “they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses” (Mat 11:8). Eli's house was chosen “to wear an ephod before me” (1Sa 2:28), and the false prophets shall no longer “wear a rough garment to deceive” (Zec 13:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wear as to carry appendant to the body, as clothes or weapons; to waste or impair by rubbing or use; to consume by degrees.
webster_full: WEAR, v.t. To waste or impair by rubbing or attrition; to lessen or diminish by continual use.
2. To carry appendant to the body, as clothes or weapons; as, to wear a coat or a robe; to wear a sword.
3. To have or exhibit an appearance; to bear; as, she wears a smile.
corruption_summary: Persecution is imagined as the sword, and Daniel's beast wears the saints out — by time, by weariness, by the slow grind of a hostile age.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 7:25 chooses its verb with care. The little horn speaks great words against the most High, thinks to change times and laws, and shall wear out the saints — the Aramaic is the word for a garment going threadbare. Most of the church's suffering in most ages has not been the stake but the grind: the steady pressure of a culture that punishes faithfulness a little every day until the faithful are simply tired. The modern believer who thinks himself unpersecuted because he has not been imprisoned should ask whether he is being worn. Exodus 18:18 gives the other side of the word: Moses was wearing away under a weight God had not asked him to carry alone, and the remedy was delegation, not endurance. Some wearing is the beast's work and must be borne; some is a man's own refusal to share a load, and must be stopped.
roots_summary: Hebrew labash (H3847), to put on, wear; nasa (H5375), to bear, wear an ephod; nabel (H5034), to wear away, fade; shachaq (H7833), to wear away by rubbing; Aramaic bela (H1080), to wear out; Greek phoreo (G5409), to wear habitually.
roots_lines: Hebrew labash (H3847) — to put on, be clothed; Deuteronomy 22:11, Zechariah 13:4, Esther 6:8.
Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to bear, carry; 1 Samuel 2:28, 22:18, “wear an ephod”; nabel (H5034), Exodus 18:18; shachaq (H7833), Job 14:19.
Aramaic bela (H1080) — to wear out, afflict; Daniel 7:25 only; Greek phoreo (G5409), Matthew 11:8.
usage: “Shall wear out the saints of the most High” — persecution by attrition.
“Thou wilt surely wear away” — Jethro's counsel to a man carrying too much.
“They that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses” — John was not one of them.

pos: interj. (an exclamation of grief, protest, or dread; rendering Hebrew ahah and hoy, Greek oua)
etymology: A natural sound, found in most languages. In the Authorized Version it belongs chiefly to Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and is the first word of a prophet's prayer under a burden.
biblical_def: Jeremiah's call begins with it: “Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child” (Jer 1:6); and his greatest prayer: “Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee” (Jer 32:17). Ezekiel cries it when told to eat defiled bread (Eze 4:14) and when the slaughter begins in Jerusalem: “Ah Lord GOD! wilt thou destroy all the residue of Israel?” (Eze 9:8). Isaiah opens with it as a woe: “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity” (Isa 1:4). At the cross it is mockery: “Ah, thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, save thyself” (Mar 15:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ah as an exclamation expressive of surprise, pity, complaint, contempt, dislike, joy, exultation, according to the manner of utterance.
webster_full: AH, an exclamation, expressive of surprise, pity, complaint, contempt, dislike, joy, exultation, &c. according to the manner of utterance.
corruption_summary: The prophet's Ah is taken for reluctance to be corrected, when it is the sound of a man who has understood the burden and prays anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: Every Ah, Lord GOD in Jeremiah and Ezekiel is a prayer that begins in protest and ends in obedience. Jeremiah says it at his call and is told, “Say not, I am a child”; he says it over the false prophets who promise peace; he says it over a field he has just bought in a doomed city, and in that prayer confesses that nothing is too hard for God and then asks how the purchase can possibly make sense. God's answer begins, “Is there any thing too hard for me?” The corruption is the modern fear of praying like this — as if a groan at the front of a prayer were unbelief. The prophets groaned at the front and believed at the back, and the Spirit, Paul says, makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. The other Ah, at the cross, is what the word becomes when it is not addressed to God: contempt shaking its head at the One who could have come down.
roots_summary: Hebrew ahah (H162), alas, ah; hoy (H1945), ah, woe; heach (H1889), aha; Greek oua (G3758), ah, an exclamation of scorn.
roots_lines: Hebrew ahah (H162) — alas, ah; Jeremiah 1:6, 4:10, 14:13, 32:17, Ezekiel 4:14, 9:8, 11:13, Joshua 7:7.
Hebrew hoy (H1945) — ah, woe, ho; Isaiah 1:4, 1:24, Jeremiah 22:18, 34:5.
Greek oua (G3758) — ah, an exclamation of derision; Mark 15:29 only.
usage: “Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak” — a prophet's call begins in protest.
“Ah Lord GOD!… there is nothing too hard for thee” — prayed after buying the field.
“Ah, thou that destroyest the temple” — the same word at the cross, without the prayer.

pos: interj. (an exclamation of malicious triumph; rendering Hebrew heach)
etymology: A doubled ah. In the Authorized Version it is always in the mouth of an enemy watching the righteous fall, and God always answers it.
biblical_def: David's enemies “opened their mouth wide against me, and said, Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it” (Psa 35:21); he prays that they “be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha” (Psa 40:15; Psa 70:3). Ammon said “Aha” against the sanctuary when it was profaned (Eze 25:3); Tyre said “Aha, she is broken that was the gates of the people” against Jerusalem (Eze 26:2); Edom said “Aha, even the ancient high places are ours in possession” over the mountains of Israel (Eze 36:2). The idolater warms himself at his fire and says, “Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire” (Isa 44:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines aha as an exclamation expressing triumph, contempt, or simple surprise.
webster_full: AHA, an exclamation expressing triumph, contempt, or simple surprise; but the senses are distinguished by very different modes of utterance, and different modifications of features.
corruption_summary: The pleasure taken in a Christian's fall is called candour, and Scripture records it as the word for which Tyre and Edom were judged.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel's oracles against the nations turn on a single syllable. Ammon, Tyre, and Edom are not judged in those chapters for invading Israel; they are judged for saying Aha when Israel fell — for the pleasure of watching. “Because thou saidst, Aha, against my sanctuary… therefore” (Eze 25:3–4). The world's aha at the church's scandals is the same word, and the church's aha at a rival's fall is worse, because Proverbs 24:17 was written to her: “Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth.” Psalm 35 is what the righteous do instead of saying it: they take the aha of their enemies to God and leave the desolating to Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew heach (H1889), aha, an exclamation of joy or malice.
roots_lines: Hebrew heach (H1889) — aha; Psalm 35:21, 35:25, 40:15, 70:3, Isaiah 44:16, Ezekiel 25:3, 26:2, 36:2, Job 39:25.
usage: “Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it” — the enemy's pleasure at the righteous man's fall.
“Because thou saidst, Aha” — the charge against Ammon, Tyre, and Edom.
“Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire” — the idolater satisfied with the half he burned.
